clue.text: Shed providing disreputable shelter beside the street

blocks.note: a dive is a seedy bar or club
ST is the usual abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A shabby lean-to put up next to the road, offered as a garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed' reads as a noun, a hut, but it is the verb: to get rid of.
explanation.definitionFit: To divest is to strip off or get rid of something, just as a tree sheds its leaves.

clue.text: See the bishop's concern

blocks.note: first meaning: a see is the area a bishop governs
second meaning: the district a bishop is responsible for

explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a verb inviting you to look; it is the noun, as in the Holy See.
explanation.definitionFit: A diocese is the territory under a bishop's authority, which church usage also calls his see.

clue.text: Inconclusive steps taken to get servant

indicators.note: something inconclusive has no proper ending, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: the valeta is an old ballroom dance, a set of steps

explanation.surface: Someone takes a few hesitant, unfinished steps in order to hire a servant.
explanation.walkthrough: The valeta (also veleta) is an old-time waltz-like dance; removing its last letter leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A valet is a personal manservant who looks after a gentleman's clothes and appearance.

clue.text: New mascot hard to put up with

indicators.note: making something new means rebuilding it, so the following word's letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A team's new mascot is hard for the fans to tolerate.
explanation.definitionFit: To stomach something is to tolerate or endure it, an idiom from swallowing food you dislike.

clue.text: It connects similar pressure points

blocks.note: surface reading: something linking the pressure points of acupuncture or massage
setter's reading: places on a weather map with equal atmospheric pressure

explanation.surface: A massage therapist describes what links the body's pressure points.
explanation.walkthrough: Pressure points suggest massage, but the pressure is barometric.
explanation.definitionFit: On a weather map, this line joins all locations sharing the same barometric reading.

clue.text: What many, in panic, make themselves

definitions.text: What many, in panic, make themselves

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it is placed inside it

blocks.note: a scare is a sudden panic
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, i.e. many

explanation.surface: When panic strikes, many people quickly make themselves scarce.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: people who panic 'make themselves scarce', i.e. run off.
explanation.definitionFit: To make oneself scarce is an idiom for leaving quickly or keeping out of the way.

clue.text: She backed the replacement of the ten-shilling note

definitions.text: She backed the replacement of the ten-shilling note

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman who supported the decision to replace a banknote

blocks.clueFragment: backed the replacement of the ten-shilling note
blocks.note: setter's reading: the female figure on the reverse of the fifty-pence coin, which replaced the ten-shilling note in 1969

explanation.surface: A woman championed the scrapping of an old banknote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' means appeared on the back. The ten-shilling note was replaced by the 50p coin at decimalisation, and the original 50p showed the seated national figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The helmeted female personification of Britain appeared on the tails side of the original fifty-pence piece.

clue.text: Pulls out Greene's novel

indicators.note: a novel version is a new one, so the letters are put into fresh order

blocks.note: the possessive taken as letters, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A publisher withdraws a novel by Graham Greene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' suggests one of Greene's books but is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To renege is to go back on a promise or withdraw from a commitment.

clue.text: Fixed rule deciding priority in a queue?

blocks.note: first meaning: a permanent regulation, as in parliamentary procedure
second meaning, playful: the order in which people are standing in line

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical second reading, taking the phrase literally as the sequence of people standing.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliaments and banks use the phrase for a permanent instruction; literally it is the sequence of those waiting upright in line.

clue.text: List of food

blocks.note: first meaning: a register of names
second meaning: a small bread bun

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an official register of names and a small baked bread bun.

clue.text: A travelling case?

blocks.note: surface reading: a suitcase taken on a journey
setter's reading: a medical case who travels to hospital for treatment and goes home the same day

explanation.walkthrough: A 'case' is luggage on the surface, but doctors call a patient a case.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone treated at a hospital without being admitted overnight comes and goes, so is a mobile medical case.

clue.text: Girl in the bar getting drunk

indicators.note: someone drunk is muddled and unsteady, so the letters stagger into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A young woman at the pub is getting tipsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertha is a woman's given name, so it is an example of a girl in crossword terms.

clue.text: Just the same, it means you had the right money

definitions.text: it means you had the right money

blocks.note: first meaning: nothing different, as a status report

blocks.clueFragment: it means you had the right money
blocks.note: second meaning: a cashier gives nothing back when you pay the exact amount

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase reports that nothing is different, and also that a shopkeeper owes nothing back after exact payment.

clue.text: It may be adjusted for the rest of the holiday

definitions.text: It may be adjusted for the rest of the holiday

blocks.note: surface reading: the remaining days of a vacation
setter's reading: a folding seat set up so a holidaymaker can relax

explanation.walkthrough: 'The rest' means the remainder on the surface, but here it is relaxation.
explanation.definitionFit: A folding canvas seat is put up on beaches and lawns so people can lounge during their vacation.

clue.text: Young goat tipped as a winner by Stevenson

blocks.note: a kid is a young goat
to nap a horse is to tip it as the day's best bet

explanation.surface: A racing tipster picks a horse called Young Goat as the winner.
explanation.walkthrough: A nap is a racing tipster's most confident selection, so 'napped' means tipped.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote the adventure novel of that name about David Balfour, so it is a work by him.

clue.text: Responsibility we can't avoid?

blocks.note: surface reading: a duty or burden
setter's reading: a duty resting upon ourselves, which the answer says when split into two short words

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer into two words and it says the duty lies upon ourselves.
explanation.definitionFit: An onus is a burden or duty, as in the onus of proof.

clue.text: Offers to take the lot?

blocks.note: surface reading: proposals to accept everything
setter's reading: an item at auction, which buyers make offers for

explanation.walkthrough: 'The lot' sounds like everything, but at an auction a lot is a single item for sale.
explanation.definitionFit: At an auction, prices called out by buyers hoping to win an item are their bids.

clue.text: They're found in north-west Spain, worn by women

blocks.note: first meaning: a people of the western Pyrenees in northern Spain
second meaning: close-fitting bodices or corsets

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the people of the region around Bilbao and a tight-fitting women's bodice.

clue.text: Someone foolish or amusing, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the words are one possible form of something else, so their letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A description of a person who is either silly or entertaining.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignoramus is an ignorant, stupid person, Latin for 'we do not know'.

clue.text: Supervise, we hear, away from this country

indicators.note: what we hear is what is spoken, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: to oversee is to supervise

explanation.surface: A manager arranges to supervise operations from abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: Oversea is an older form of overseas, meaning abroad or in a foreign land.

clue.text: All the same, it suits some people

blocks.note: first meaning: consistent, unvarying throughout
second meaning: official clothing worn by soldiers, nurses and others

explanation.walkthrough: 'All the same' sounds like 'nevertheless', but it means identical; 'suits' is literal, clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means unvarying, and the noun is standard dress provided for police, schoolchildren or soldiers.

clue.text: A Spaniard is taken for a Greek

blocks.note: taken as written
Don is a Spanish title for a gentleman
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man from Spain is mistaken for someone from Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: Adonis is the beautiful youth of Greek mythology loved by Aphrodite.

clue.text: One naturally separated from the rest of humanity

definitions.text: One naturally separated from the rest of humanity

blocks.clueFragment: One naturally separated from the rest of humanity
blocks.note: surface reading: a born loner or misanthrope
setter's reading: someone cut off by the sea, a geographical feature

explanation.walkthrough: It sounds like a recluse by temperament; 'naturally' means by nature's geography. It echoes Donne's 'No man is an island'.
explanation.definitionFit: A person living on land surrounded by water is physically cut off from the mainland population.

clue.text: Necessitate a note before Latin revision

indicators.note: a revision reworks a text, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: E is one of the musical notes
taken as written

explanation.surface: A student must jot a note before revising for a Latin exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revision' reads as exam study but is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To entail is to involve as a necessary consequence, so it means to make something required.

clue.text: Dragged to the altar?

blocks.note: surface reading: pulled along, as by a rope or tow truck
setter's reading: split in two, the answer means going in order to marry

explanation.surface: A reluctant groom is hauled to his wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as two words, the answer names the purpose of a trip down the aisle.
explanation.definitionFit: A car hauled behind another by a rope has been pulled along, i.e. dragged.

clue.text: Uncle Sam's braces

blocks.note: surface reading: the straps holding up an American's trousers
setter's reading: the American name for what Britons call braces

explanation.walkthrough: Uncle Sam stands for the USA. British braces are trouser straps; in Britain the American word means garters holding up stockings, which is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: In American English, straps over the shoulders holding up trousers go by this name.

clue.text: One is angry having lost it

definitions.text: One is angry having lost it

blocks.clueFragment: One is angry having lost it
blocks.note: surface reading: someone furious after losing something
setter's reading: a British idiom in which losing a sheep's fleece means losing your temper

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lost it' already suggests losing your temper; the British phrase 'keep your wool on' means stay calm.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheep's fleece features in a colloquial British idiom: losing it means flying into a rage.

clue.text: Presumably he likes painstaking people

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who admires careful, meticulous workers
setter's reading: people who take pain, i.e. victims who suffer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Painstaking' means careful, but read literally it is 'pain-taking'.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a person derives pleasure from inflicting suffering on others.

clue.text: Daisy's song cycle?

blocks.note: surface reading: a series of songs by a composer called Daisy
setter's reading: the 'bicycle built for two' in the song Daisy Bell

explanation.walkthrough: A song cycle is a set of songs, but here cycle is a bicycle: 'Daisy, Daisy' ends with a bicycle built for two.
explanation.definitionFit: The music-hall song describes a two-seater bicycle, which is exactly this machine.
